transcript.content: A man in his fifties with two hours of central pressure that eased by the time he reached us. First ECG shows only nonspecific lateral T flattening. We're a district hospital with a conventional troponin, no high-sensitivity assay, and the PCI centre is a long ambulance ride away. He's diabetic and was reluctant to come in at all. I lean towards unstable angina because the pressure came on while he was walking and settled at rest. With a negative first troponin and a low HEART score, do I discharge him, or keep him for a repeat and transfer, and what does that hinge on with our assay?

Not on a single negative conventional troponin this early. With pain starting about two hours ago, the first sample can be falsely reassuring, so a later repeat is needed (ESC guidelines, 2020).
- A HEART score of three or fewer identifies a low-risk group in which early discharge is safe (HEART score, 2013).
- Diabetes and exertional pressure push the history and risk-factor points up, so he may not score low at all.
❓ How would you score his history and risk factors honestly, and would that number change your plan?

You said a score of three or fewer makes early discharge safe. Which patients was that low-risk group drawn from, and was anyone like him in it? He lives far out, has already told us he won't come back once he's home, and I don't have cardiology on site to review him.

Good question, and I stated that too broadly. The HEART score was developed and tested in emergency department cohorts with hospital follow-up (HEART score, 2013). It ranks risk; it does not tell you whether a man who lives far away will come back if his pain returns. For him a low score would not make discharge safe, and with his risk factors it would not be low.
❓ Does your lab's troponin assay support a one-hour rule-out pathway at all, or only a later repeat?

Our assay is conventional, so there is no one-hour pathway for us, only a later repeat. His mild kidney impairment may keep the baseline raised, and he takes metformin, which the dye would complicate if he does go on to the PCI centre. If I give aspirin now, does the anticoagulant wait for the repeat, or is waiting just delay?

Right, the one-hour algorithms are validated for high-sensitivity assays, so with a conventional assay stay with a later repeat (ESC guidelines, 2023). A chronically raised baseline from kidney disease is a real issue, and the change between samples is the better signal.
- Aspirin can be given now when ACS is suspected; no need to wait for the repeat (ESC guidelines, 2023).
- Parenteral anticoagulation is recommended once NSTE-ACS is diagnosed, so it can follow the repeat result (ESC guidelines, 2023).
❓ What would make you start anticoagulation before the repeat?

Established: aspirin now. Validated as a risk ranking only: the HEART group, drawn from emergency departments with follow-up, with nothing showing discharge is safe for a man who can't return. No source I know of: anticoagulant timing for a nondiagnostic ECG on a conventional assay, since those trials enrolled confirmed or biomarker-positive patients. Holding him for the repeat, transfer centre on standby.

Reasonable. The HEART score is a validated risk ranking, not a trial-proven discharge rule for patients with poor follow-up (HEART score, 2013), and anticoagulant timing in conventional-assay patients rests largely on consensus (ESC guidelines, 2023). Holding him for the repeat is defensible, with transfer ready in parallel.
❓ How reliable is the onset time you have for him?

He can't say exactly; the pressure began while he walked in from the car park and had eased by the time he sat down in the cubicle. You said an early first sample can be falsely reassuring, so the clock matters. When onset is vague, do I count the repeat interval from arrival?

If onset is vague, do not count from the earliest guess; time the repeat from arrival and give it the full interval, because a repeat that is too early can be falsely reassuring (ESC guidelines, 2020). Hold him at least until it is back, and keep transfer ready to start the moment it rises or the pain recurs.
❓ What would you tell him about returning if he insists on going home before the repeat?

เรียนรู้อะไร / What I learned:
I came in treating a low HEART score as permission to discharge. It is a risk ranking tested where patients can return and cardiology is on site, and our assay is not the one the one-hour pathway was built for. The repeat sample, timed from onset or from arrival, matters more for us than the score. Aspirin does not wait; anticoagulation can.

ความไม่แน่นอน / What remains uncertain:
Whether a repeat after three hours on a conventional assay is enough for a man who won't return, and how to count when onset is vague. I have not found a trial that answers it for a district hospital.

จะตรวจสอบ/นำไปใช้อย่างไร / How I will verify or apply it:
On Monday I will pull our last chest pain discharges with a single troponin and see how many came back within a week, ask the lab for the assay's cut-off and imprecision at the low end, and draft a one-page pathway with the transfer centre that fixes who calls whom when onset time is unclear.
